cues.text: Section eight: Strategic resource allocation and human capital.
Let us begin with resources.
Resources in an organisation include money, people, time, infrastructure, data and expertise.
Because these are scarce, organisations must make trade-offs.
This brings us to opportunity cost, which is the value of the best alternative that is forgone when a choice is made.
Consider an example: if scarce AI specialists are allocated to a low-value experiment, that choice may delay a critical project that needed them.
Next, we look at how allocation is managed over time.
Dynamic resource planning means adjusting allocation as priorities, demand and evidence change.
Stage-gating is a related practice, in which projects are reviewed before any further funding is released.
Dependency mapping identifies prerequisites and shared bottlenecks, so that planners can see what must happen first and where several efforts compete for the same limited resource.
Cross-training improves flexibility, because people can cover more than one kind of work.
And subcontracting fills temporary expertise gaps, when the organisation needs a skill only for a limited period.
Now consider human capital.
Human capital management includes skills inventories, recruitment, training, succession planning, workload management and retention.
An important caution applies here: more staff do not automatically accelerate work.
Onboarding and coordination consume capacity, so new people may initially add overhead before they add output.
This leads us to the idea of a bottleneck.
A bottleneck is a constraint that limits overall throughput.
Suppose a team can develop ten features weekly, but testing can validate only four.
In that case, the pipeline cannot sustainably deliver ten features a week.
Adding more developers may simply increase work in progress rather than output, since the extra work just queues in front of testing.
To address a bottleneck, you diagnose queues, cycle times, utilisation, dependencies and rework.
Then you improve the constraint, through training, automation, prioritisation or capacity adjustment, and afterwards you reassess, because the constraint may have moved elsewhere.
Finally, we turn to value stream mapping, abbreviated VSM.
Value stream mapping visualises end-to-end work and information flow, and it identifies value-adding activities, waiting and waste.
Here is a worked example.
Suppose a cloud provisioning request requires two hours of actual work, but waits 46 hours for approvals.
The lead time is 48 hours, and the processing time is two hours.
Flow efficiency is the processing time divided by the lead time: two divided by forty-eight, which is approximately 4.17 percent.
The lesson is that streamlining the approval step may deliver more benefit than accelerating the provisioning code, because nearly all of the elapsed time is spent waiting rather than working.
